source: Shin, Polyanskaya, Lucero, Oulasvirta (2025) No Evidence for LLMs Being Useful in Problem Reframing
finding: Large blinded online experiment on design problem reframing. Using GPT-4o in any of three ways did not make the best problem frames more novel or more useful than frames written by people alone.
numbers: 456 recruited, 280 kept after filtering. Four between-subject arms: manual, direct (LLM frames), free-form (chat), structured (Dorst nine-step process). Mann-Whitney (manual vs all LLM) and Kruskal-Wallis with Dunn post hoc: no significant difference in novelty or usefulness. Power analysis: 220 and 280 needed for a medium effect at 95% power. Frames rated by 15 high-expertise designers.
quote: using LLMs does not help improve the quality of problem frames
limits: Crowd workers, one session, GPT-4o only, 2 reframing problems, best frame chosen by participant, rated by few experts. Null result with power only for a medium effect, so small effects are not excluded.
agent_relevance: Adding an LLM to reframing is not a free gain. The one large test of O8-style reframing is null, so O8 should be gated by an outside test or failure signal, not applied by default.

source: Shin, Polyanskaya, Lucero, Oulasvirta (2025) No Evidence for LLMs Being Useful in Problem Reframing (expertise moderator)
finding: Expertise changed who gained. Experts at reframing made more novel frames than novices when an LLM was used, so LLM help may widen the gap rather than close it.
numbers: LLM-conditioned frames: experts +12.54% novelty vs novices (z=2.70, p=0.01). Largest in free-form arm (+20.84%) but not significant (p=0.06). No usefulness gap (all p>0.05). Agency: experts felt more agency (z=2.05, p=0.04); structured arm +15.69% (z=2.29, p=0.02). Expert/novice split = 3 or more of 5 quiz items correct; chi-square on assignment p=0.87.
limits: Post hoc subgroup, expertise measured by a short quiz, effects on perception not quality. The arXiv abstract states the agency effect the other way round for novices; the body text gives experts more agency.
agent_relevance: A weak or unguided reframing step may help only when the model already has a good criterion for choosing among frames. Selection by a code check matters more than generation.

source: Shin, Polyanskaya, Lucero, Oulasvirta (2025) No Evidence for LLMs Being Useful in Problem Reframing (structured process and perception gap)
finding: Following the nine-step frame creation process of Dorst with LLM help did not beat the other arms. People still rated the LLM tools as helpful, so felt help and measured quality came apart.
numbers: Creativity Support Index: direct 64.28 (SD 18.90), structured 64.85 (SD 20.00), free-form 61.01 (SD 17.19); scores 50-90 count as good support; no difference between arms. Mean time to produce 2 frames: manual 23.25 min, direct 21.82, structured 28.35, free-form 20.78. In structured arm all but one participant regenerated all content at least once.
limits: Perceived helpfulness is self-report. Structured arm took longest but gained nothing.
agent_relevance: Do not trust the model or a user feeling that a reframe helped. Score reframes by task outcome.

source: Dorst and Cross (2001) Creativity in the design process: co-evolution of problem-solution
finding: Protocol study of nine experienced industrial designers. Creativity was linked to how the designer formulated the problem, and problem space and solution space developed together. Authors confirm the co-evolution model and add default and surprise spaces.
numbers: 9 experienced industrial designers, protocol analysis, designs rated on overall quality and on creativity. Full-paper numbers (rating distribution, per-designer scores) not retrieved.
limits: Only the abstract page was read this session; the PDF was not reachable (403 or host unreachable). Nine designers, one brief, ratings by judges, no control group, so no causal claim that reframing causes creativity.
agent_relevance: Support for O8 is correlational and from a very small sample. Treat frame shift then creative solution as a plausible pattern, not a measured effect size.

source: Sio, Kotovsky, Cagan (2015) Fixation or inspiration? A meta-analytic review of the role of examples on design processes
finding: The standard meta-analysis of whether showing example designs fixates designers or inspires them. Only its existence and bibliographic data were confirmed.
numbers: Crossref record confirmed: Design Studies vol 39, pp 70-99, 63 references. Effect sizes and study counts not retrieved (publisher page returned 403, no abstract in Crossref).
limits: Not opened. Do not quote effect sizes from this line.
agent_relevance: Follow-up needed: pull the effect sizes before using fixation as a reason for or against showing the agent worked examples.

source: Youmans and Arciszewski (2014) Design fixation: classifications and modern methods of prevention
finding: Conceptual review that splits fixation into three classes (unconscious adherence to prior designs, conscious blocks to change, intentional resistance) and two types (concept-based, knowledge-based).
numbers: No experimental numbers. AI EDAM vol 28 issue 2, pp 129-137.
limits: Abstract page only (full text paywalled). A taxonomy, not evidence of what works.
agent_relevance: Frame persistence has more than one cause. Only the unconscious kind is likely to respond to a forced reframe prompt.

source: Jansson and Smith (1991) Design fixation, as summarised by Wadinambiarachchi et al. (2024)
finding: Classic fixation result: groups shown an example solution produced about as many designs as controls, but their designs copied more features of the example.
numbers: Four experiments in the original; per the secondary source, fixation and control groups had similar design counts, and fixation-group ideas were more similar to the example.
limits: Original not read; described through a 2024 paper. Replication record of the original experiments not checked.
agent_relevance: An example in the prompt narrows the frame of the agent at no cost to output volume. Count distinct approaches, not the number of answers.

source: Wadinambiarachchi, Kelly, Pareek, Zhou, Velloso (2024) The Effects of Generative AI on Design Fixation and Divergent Thinking
finding: Seeing AI-generated images before sketching increased fixation on an example design more than image search did, compared with no inspiration support.
numbers: 60 designers, between-subject, chatbot-avatar sketching in 20 min, 14 coded features from the example. Bayesian binomial model (probit): GenAI +0.32 (89% CI .11 to .55, Bayes factor 124); Image search +0.27 (89% CI .05 to .49, BF 42.48); intercept -0.71.
limits: Midjourney V4 only, one task, student sample, fixation measured by feature copying. Other outcomes (fluency, variety, originality) were also modelled but not extracted here.
agent_relevance: An LLM that proposes frames can anchor the agent or the user on them. Hold the first frame lightly and compare against a frame made without the model suggestion.

source: Deng, Zhang, Chen, Gu (2023) Rephrase and Respond: Let Large Language Models Ask Better Questions for Themselves
finding: Letting GPT-4 rewrite an ambiguous question and then answer it raised accuracy a lot on tasks where the question was poorly framed for the model.
numbers: GPT-4 zero-shot, original vs RaR: even-day 54.29 to 93.33; even-month 58.10 to 83.96; even-year 57.14 to 89.52. Last-letter concatenation with CoT: one-shot 89.04 to 100; four-shot 87.21 to 100. Zero-shot CoT on Chinese idioms scored 31.43%, worse than RaR.
limits: 10 tasks, mostly synthetic or constructed for the paper, GPT-4 mid-2023 snapshots, ambiguity partly the fault of the human prompt. Gain is about clarifying a question, not about changing the frame of the problem.
agent_relevance: Cheap rewrite-then-answer helps most when the prompt is ambiguous. It is better evidenced than free self-reflection, but it is clarification, not O8.

source: Deng et al. (2023) RaR: model-capacity moderator
finding: Rewriting helped stronger models more. Weaker models gained little and sometimes lost accuracy, and a strong model rewrite helped a weak model answer.
numbers: Two-step RaR on GPT-4-0613, GPT-3.5-turbo-0613 and Vicuna-13b-v1.5: GPT-4 gains largest; GPT-3.5 and Vicuna slightly worse on the Sports task. Vicuna own rephrasings seldom clarified; GPT-4-written rephrasings improved Vicuna answers.
limits: Bar-chart values only partly legible in extracted text; direction and ordering are reliable, exact deltas for GPT-3.5 and Vicuna not extracted.
agent_relevance: A reframe step is worth running only if the model is strong enough to produce a real reframe; otherwise it adds drift. Check by a held-out test.

source: Zheng, Gui, Zhang, Huang, et al. (2024) Self-Polish: Enhance Reasoning in Large Language Models via Problem Refinement
finding: Having the model rewrite a math word problem into a cleaner one before solving gave small average gains, with some losses.
numbers: text-davinci-003, chain-of-thought average over 5 sets: none 62.6, in-context SP 63.7 (+1.1), Auto-SP 63.4 (+0.8), Complex-SP 64.0 (+1.4). GSM8K CoT 56.1 to 56.7/56.9/58.1. MultiArith CoT 90.8 to 88.5/89.7/90.2 (loss). Least-to-most average 61.4 to 63.3/62.9/64.3.
limits: Old GPT-3 family models (text-davinci-002/003, GPT-3.5-Turbo); gains of 1 to 3 points are inside typical prompt noise; a failure case shows the rewrite changing the meaning of the question.
agent_relevance: Problem rewriting that stays inside the same frame gives about 1 point. A rewrite can silently change the question, so check the new problem still entails the old one.

source: Zheng, Mishra, Chen, et al. (2023) Take a Step Back: Evoking Reasoning via Abstraction in Large Language Models
finding: Asking the model first for the general principle behind a question, then answering, gave large gains on physics, chemistry and time-sensitive QA. This is abstraction (O2) rather than a new frame of the goal, but it is the strongest LLM result for stepping back.
numbers: PaLM-2L: MMLU physics 66.4 to 73.2, chemistry 70.9 to 81.8. GPT-4 physics 69.4 to 84.5, chemistry 80.9 to 85.6. Llama2-70B physics 51.9 to 64.8, chemistry 55.7 to 66.7. TimeQA PaLM-2L 41.5 baseline, 57.4 RAG, 66 step-back, 68.7 step-back plus RAG. On MMLU physics step-back fixed 20.5% of baseline errors and introduced 11.9%.
limits: Averages over 5 runs with SDs; model-graded evaluation; most remaining errors are in the reasoning step, not the abstraction step. Table row-to-model mapping read from extracted text and may be off by one row for GPT-4 versus Llama2.
agent_relevance: Backs O2 more than O8. Note the 11.9% newly broken answers: a stepped-back frame also breaks answers that were right, so keep the original answer as a candidate.

source: Zhou et al. (2024) Self-Discover: Large Language Models Self-Compose Reasoning Structures
finding: Letting the model pick and combine reasoning modules for each task type (a task-level change of method) beat chain-of-thought on most of 25 tasks, with 10 to 40 times less compute than self-consistency.
numbers: BBH 23 tasks: +7 points over CoT and +6 over plan-and-solve on PaLM-2L, +6 and +8 on GPT-4. T4D: 69% (PaLM-2L) and 85% (GPT-4) vs 30 to 42% and 51 to 53% for baselines. MATH: gain of 1 to 7 points (PaLM-2L), 2 to 3 (GPT-4). Better than CoT on 21 of 25 tasks. Gains largest on world-knowledge tasks, smaller on algorithmic ones.
limits: Method choice, not goal reframing. Task-level structure is built once from unlabeled examples. Closed models, 2023 versions.
agent_relevance: Choosing the approach at task level before solving instance by instance is cheap and has support. It differs from O8, which acts on the failed attempt.

source: Mishra, Khashabi, Baral, Choi, Hajishirzi (2022) Reframing Instructional Prompts to GPTk Language
finding: Hand-rewriting task instructions into short, concrete, itemised, decomposed forms raised GPT-3 scores on 12 tasks.
numbers: ROUGE-L with GPT3-instruct: few-shot 44 to 58 (+14 absolute), zero-shot 33 to 50 (+17). Reframed prompts also beat a schema-selection baseline by 11 (47 to 58) in few-shot. Five techniques: pattern reflection, itemizing, decomposing, restraining, specialising.
limits: Manual rewriting by the authors on a fixed task set with a 2022 model; reframing here means rewording the instruction, not changing the goal. No tests on current models.
agent_relevance: Wording and format are a big lever, so any measured gain from a reframe step must be compared with simple rewording controls.

source: Sclar, Choi, Tsvetkov, Suhr (2024) Quantifying Language Models Sensitivity to Spurious Features in Prompt Design
finding: Meaning-preserving changes to prompt format moved accuracy by up to 76 points, and size, shots or instruction tuning did not remove this.
numbers: LLaMA-2-13B spread up to 76 accuracy points between equivalent formats; about 10 points on average across 50+ tasks and several models; sensitivity remained with larger models, more few-shot examples and instruction tuning.
limits: Mostly open models of 2023, few-shot classification tasks. Newer models may be less sensitive; not tested here.
agent_relevance: Any claim that a reframe lifted accuracy needs a format-variance baseline. A single before and after pair can be noise of 10 points.

source: Li et al. (2025) Solving Situation Puzzles with Large Language Model and External Reformulation
finding: In lateral-thinking puzzles, restarting the chat with the puzzle rewritten to include the confirmed facts from earlier Q&A let the player win more often with fewer questions.
numbers: 5 puzzles, max 30 questions and 5 guesses. Baseline vs reformulation (K=5 questions, M=3 facts kept): win/lose 2/3 vs 4/1; guesses 2.8 vs 2.4; questions 28.6 vs 22.6; yes-questions 3.6 vs 5; no-questions 18.2 vs 12.2; irrelevant 6.8 vs 5.4. Ablation: K=5/M=3 best; end-on-wrong-guess-only and K=10/M=6 worse.
limits: Only 5 puzzles, one game run each, so win/lose 4/1 vs 2/3 is a difference of two games and carries no statistical weight. Model details not recorded in the extracted text.
agent_relevance: Plausible pattern for O8: when stuck in a long dialogue, restart from a fresh summary of confirmed facts. Needs a real test before adoption; this is anecdote-sized.

source: Jiang, Ilievski, Ma, Sourati (2023) BRAINTEASER: Lateral Thinking Puzzles for Large Language Models
finding: On puzzles whose answer needs breaking the default commonsense frame, the best model sat halfway between chance and humans, and fell further on rewritten versions of the same puzzles.
numbers: 1,119 items (sentence and word puzzles). ChatGPT 53% and 63% on the two subtasks; random 25%; humans 92%. ChatGPT and RoBERTa-L failed 45% and 61% of originals or semantic variants that they solved in the context-reconstruction version. Human performance dropped little on group-consistency metrics, models dropped a lot. Commonsense fine-tuning hurt sentence puzzles.
limits: ChatGPT 2023 only, multiple choice (can be solved for wrong reasons), memorisation likely for famous puzzles. Needs rerun on current models.
agent_relevance: Models stick to the default frame and are inconsistent when the same puzzle is reworded, so a reframe step must be tested across rewordings, not on single items.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: Without outside feedback, asking a model to review and revise its own answer lowers accuracy. Gains seen earlier came from leaking the correct label.
numbers: GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 to 75.1 (round 1) to 74.7 (round 2); CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 38.1 to 41.8; HotpotQA 26.0 to 25.0. GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 91.5 to 89.0; CSQA 82.0 to 79.5 to 80.0; HotpotQA 49 to 49 to 43. With oracle labels GPT-3.5 GSM8K 84.3. GPT-3.5 kept its answer 74.7% of the time on GSM8K.
limits: 2023 models; the main claim is for intrinsic self-correction without feedback or tools.
agent_relevance: A reframe that is triggered by the doubt of the model will mostly not fire correctly. Trigger O8 from a code-checked failure.

source: Qi, Lee, Breazeal, Park (2025) Does Reasoning with LLMs Improve Recognizing, Generating and Reframing Unhelpful Thoughts?
finding: On clinical cognitive reframing, GPT-3.5 with prompting methods beat reasoning-trained models such as DeepSeek-R1 and o1 on spotting distortions, and generally did well on reframing tasks.
numbers: PatternReframe, 1,000 examples, 100 per thinking pattern. Task 1 (recognise distortion): GPT-3.5 plus Diagnosis-of-Thought beat R1 and o1 by about 40 points of accuracy. Compared non-reasoning (GPT-3.5, 4, 4o), pretrained reasoning (Llama-3.3, R1, o1, o3-mini) and augmented reasoning (CoT, ToT, self-consistency, DoT).
limits: Therapy-style reframing of a thought of a person, not reframing of a task goal. Task-specific prompt (DoT) drives Task 1. Automatic metrics (ROUGE, BERTScore) for generation tasks.
agent_relevance: Reasoning-trained models are not automatically better at reframing; the kind of reframing prompt matters. Keep the reframe step explicit and typed.

source: Sharma, Rushton, Lin, Wadden, Lucas, Miner, Nguyen, Althoff (2023) Cognitive Reframing of Negative Thoughts through Human-Language Model Interaction
finding: In a large field study on a mental-health site, people preferred reframes that were empathic and specific and liked overly positive ones less. Safety review flagged very few outputs.
numbers: Preferred more often: high empathy 39.7% vs 25.5% (p<1e-5); high specificity 39.2% vs 27.4%; high positivity preferred less, 29.6% vs 38.3%. Ratings (1 to 5): high rationality more relatable 3.91 vs 3.53 (p<0.05); reframes addressing thinking traps more helpful 3.39 vs 3.19 (p<0.01); high actionability more memorable 3.67 vs 3.40. 32 of 5,760 suggestions flagged (0.56%).
limits: Preference and self-rating, not symptom change. Single platform, English only.
agent_relevance: A good reframe is concrete and checkable, not just more positive. For our agent: a reframe that names a specific different subgoal beats a vague rewording.

source: Graf, Danek, et al. (2023) Tracing Cognitive Processes in Insight Problem Solving: GAMs and Change Point Analysis
finding: Eye-movement data on matchstick arithmetic show a sudden shift of attention to the critical operator in people who solve, and ordinary ANOVA misses the abruptness. An explicit hint changes how attention moves.
numbers: Only 34% solved within 5 minutes. After the hint (you can change the operators, too) an extra 11% solved. Dwell time on the critical plus sign roughly doubled by the 20% time bin after the hint. Nonlinear models (GAMs, change-point analysis) found the abrupt change; classical ANOVA did not.
limits: One problem type, lab sample, eye tracking; the hint was given to non-solvers only. Author list beyond the first two not checked.
agent_relevance: Reframing can be a sudden switch, which a step-by-step log may hide. A direct hint on which element can change is a strong, cheap intervention.

source: Spiridonov, Erofeeva, Klowait, Morozov, Ardislamov (2026) The modulating role of sources of difficulty in interactive matchstick algebra
finding: A failed conceptual replication of the claim that physical interaction boosts insight in matchstick algebra. Participants did not move the sticks much, and when they did, movement hurt constraint relaxation instead of helping.
numbers: Three experiments, n=54, 45 and 45. Mean movements in Exp 1: problem A 0.56, B 1.70, C 1.91, D 8.26. Only the VR interactive-sticks condition showed clear evidence of an effect, accuracy about 92% (+6 percentage points). Motor activity did not help chunk decomposition and interfered with relaxing higher-level constraints. Bayesian logistic regression, so null evidence can be quantified.
limits: Conceptual (not exact) replication of Weller et al. 2011; small cells (20 to 25); the original interactive condition and interactive solution were mixed up in the original, so the claim is narrower than first thought.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: what unlocks a reframe depends on the type of block (perceptual chunk vs high-level constraint). One generic reframe instruction cannot be expected to fix both.

source: Weller et al. (2011) interactivity in matchstick algebra; Knoblich et al. (1999) representational change, as described by Spiridonov et al. (2026)
finding: Original theory: insight difficulty comes from two sources, relaxing high-level constraints and decomposing perceptual chunks, and problem types A to D differ in which they require. Interactivity was reported to raise success on harder types (B, C, D), not on A, and later work (Vallee-Tourangeau 2015, 2016; Henok 2020) was reported as consistent with it.
numbers: No numbers from the originals; secondary description only. Problem type C needs constraint relaxation; D needs both.
limits: Original papers not opened. The claim about interactivity is the one the 2026 replication failed to reproduce.
agent_relevance: Gives the discriminating prediction for reframing studies: ask which kind of block a problem has before choosing the reframing move (O4 for constraints, O6 for chunks).

source: Bianchi and Branchini (2023) Does Thinking in Opposites in Order to Think Differently Improve Creativity?
finding: Review of studies where people were told, or trained, to list the properties of the problem and flip each into its opposite. In each of three studies that tested it, success on spatial insight problems beat controls. Benefit was found in small groups.
numbers: Three studies (Branchini 2015a, Branchini 2016, Bianchi 2020) with hint and training arms all based on opposites: higher success than controls in every arm, no pooled effect size given. Trained participants showed less fixedness and searched both ways (splitting what was joined, joining what was split). The review notes hints and training worked only in small group settings in the 2015a and 2016 studies.
limits: A review by the same group that ran the studies; spatial insight problems only; no meta-analytic effect size; individual-solver effects not shown in the quoted text.
agent_relevance: Candidate content for O8: list the features of the framing and flip each one. Evidence is narrow (spatial puzzles) and from one lab, so test before trusting.

source: PLOS ONE (2026) Generative AI as a cognitive support tool in early-stage design ideation: a human-AI co-ideation experiment
finding: In a within-subject test with 32 design students, the AI-assisted condition scored far higher on rated problem framing and ideation breadth, but the human-only condition scored higher on innovation and solution strategy.
numbers: Paired t-tests (df 31), Holm-corrected: problem framing AI 4.64 vs human 2.94 (dz 2.48); mechanism 4.48 vs 2.99 (dz 2.49); creator perspective 4.03 vs 3.55 (dz 0.90); evaluator perspective 4.25 vs 3.26 (dz 1.53); innovation human 4.66 vs AI 3.40 (dz 2.69); solution strategies 4.22 vs 3.67 (dz 1.47). No robust difference on form, material, color, pattern; style p=.050, dz 0.36.
limits: Three raters, task-specific rubric where problem framing means clarity of defining the problem, which is not the same as Dorst-style frame creation. The AI arm used a fixed text-and-image workflow, and effect sizes this large (dz above 2) suggest rubric and format effects.
agent_relevance: An LLM can make the problem statement clearer and more structured, yet it may lower rated innovation. Clear framing is not the same as a new frame.
